summary: After Earth is an interactive 3D Mars outpost simulation and STEM educational web game built for students and young learners. Players act as mission engineers—scouting landing zones on a 3D Mars Globe, building pressurized habitats, prospecting for water with a 6-wheeled rover, and surviving dust storms, radiation spikes, and marsquakes alongside an expressive AI companion drone, A.S.T.R.O.Rather than relying on fictional mechanics, the simulation integrates 11 official NASA Planetary Data System (PDS) instruments alongside the NASA Mars Fact Sheet directly into gameplay. NASA MOLA laser altimetry reconstructs Jezero Crater (18.38° N, 77.58° E, -2,540m) and evaluates terrain slopes (< 5° safe vs. > 15° hazardous), while MRO HiRISE data (25–30 cm/pixel) assesses surface boulder hazards during landing. For prospecting, 2001 Mars Odyssey GRS maps shallow hydrogen (1m depth), MRO SHARAD radar profiles deeper ice layers (1m–1km) via the rover's drill, MRO CRISM highlights Hematite ore and hydrated clays, and Odyssey THEMIS powers infrared night-vision thermal scanning.   Outpost survival relies on surface mission telemetry. Perseverance's MOXIE experiment models converting Mars's 95.3% CO2 atmosphere into oxygen, while Phoenix MECA and Curiosity SAM soil findings require players to wash toxic perchlorates (0.5%–1%) from regolith before greenhouse farming.
details:
What It Does

After Earth is an interactive 3D Mars outpost simulation and STEM educational web game designed for students and young learners. Players step into the role of a Martian mission engineer to scout landing sites from orbit, touch down on the Red Planet, mine local resources, construct a pressurized modular habitat, prospect for subsurface water with a 6-wheeled rover, and survive real Martian hazards—including severe dust storms, solar radiation spikes, and marsquakes—guided by an expressive AI companion drone named A.S.T.R.O.

How It Works

Orbital Reconnaissance & Free Global Landing: Players begin on an interactive, Google Earth-style 3D Mars Globe built from real NASA elevation and surface imagery datasets. They inspect terrain slopes, boulder hazards, and mineral signatures across Mars before choosing any coordinates to initiate orbital descent.

Guided Onboarding & 5-Stage Engineering Campaign: A step-by-step interactive tutorial with 3D waypoint beacons teaches movement (0.38g Martian gravity), geological scanning, resource harvesting, modular building, and power management before unlocking five escalating missions:

Mission 1 — The Landing: Analyze orbital topography (MOLA) and surface roughness (HiRISE) to execute a safe touchdown.

Mission 2 — Build Your Base: Harvest regolith, water ice, and hematite ore to snap-build and seal a pressurized base (Habitat Core, Airlock, 3×2 Solar Arrays, Battery Bank, MOXIE oxygen generator, Water Processor, Geodesic Bio-Dome Greenhouse, and Research Lab).

Mission 3 — The Water Mystery: Drive a 6-wheeled Pressurized Mars Rover equipped with a subsurface radar drill (SHARAD) to investigate orbital hydrogen anomalies (Odyssey GRS), analyze core samples in the Research Lab, and separate false-positive hydrated clays from true extractable water-ice aquifers.

Mission 4 — Dust Storm Survival: Respond to a 45-second storm warning as atmospheric dust opacity (MEDA Tau) surges—triaging non-essential power loads in the Power Distribution Console, relying on battery reserves, and manually brushing dust off solar wings.

Mission 5 — Radiation Threat: Track live radiation spikes (Curiosity RAD) during a Solar Particle Event and reinforce habitat walls with 3D-printed regolith shielding (≥ 85%) to protect the crew.

Real-Time NASA Telemetry & Context-Aware AI Companion: Eleven NASA Planetary Data System (PDS) instruments and physical Martian constants drive the simulation's environment, scanner modes (including THEMIS thermal infrared vision), soil perchlorate remediation (MECA/SAM), and CO₂-to-O₂ electrolysis (MOXIE). A.S.T.R.O. appears dynamically at key moments with an animated LED visor face to deliver real NASA facts, mission briefings, and disaster consequence alerts.

Its Benefits

Hands-On STEM & Systems Thinking: Transforms abstract planetary science and aerospace engineering trade-offs—such as shutting down a research lab to keep oxygen generators running during a dust storm—into intuitive, cause-and-effect survival decisions for students and children.

Authentic Scientific Literacy: Connects gameplay directly to 11 real NASA datasets and instruments, helping learners understand how planetary scientists actually map water, measure radiation, and plan human habitats on Mars.

Zero-Barrier Classroom Accessibility: Built to run directly inside standard desktop web browsers at 60 FPS with no downloads, installations, or specialized hardware required, making it immediately deployable in schools and STEM workshops.

Inclusive UX & Multi-Input Support: Features clean, high-legibility typography (Outfit and Cairo), concise student-friendly explanations, collapsible HUD panels, and seamless support for both Keyboard/Mouse and Xbox Controllers (with analog navigation and haptic rumble feedback).

Tools, Languages, Hardware, and Software Used

Programming Languages: TypeScript (strict: true), HTML5, CSS3, GLSL (custom atmospheric and planetary shaders), and JavaScript / Node.js (for DEM elevation map preprocessing).

3D Engine, Web Frameworks & APIs:

Three.js: Real-time WebGL 3D rendering, custom terrain chunking, raycasting, instanced resource meshes, procedural PBR canvas textures, and dynamic lighting/shadows.

Vite: Fast module bundling and development build pipeline.

Web Audio API: Procedural sound synthesis (UI micro-ticks, mining impacts, mechanical build snaps) and adaptive ambient soundscape crossfading.

HTML5 Gamepad API: Plug-and-play Xbox Controller input mapping and dual-rumble haptic feedback.

NASA Data Sources & Science Tooling:

NASA Planetary Data System (PDS): MOLA (MGS), HiRISE, CRISM, and SHARAD (MRO), GRS and THEMIS (2001 Mars Odyssey), RAD and SAM (Curiosity MSL), MEDA and MOXIE (Perseverance Mars 2020), SEIS (InSight), and MECA (Phoenix).

NASA NSSDC Mars Fact Sheet: Planetary gravity, atmospheric pressure, solar irradiance, and Sol cycle constants.

Software & Design Tools: Visual Studio Code, Google Antigravity IDE, Canva & Figma (UI layout, mission badges, and emblem branding), OBS Studio & audio/video editing tools (intro story cutscene and ambient audio), and Git / GitHub.

Hardware: Standard Windows 11 development laptop/workstation and an Xbox Wireless Controller for dual-input testing.
